newsitem.title: USA: IMF board sets $48 billion fund for emergencies.
newsitem.headline: IMF board sets $48 billion fund for emergencies.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund's executive board on Monday agreed to establish a $48 billion war-chest to help the lending agency fight economic crises so serious they threatened the global monetary system.
Called the New Arrangements to Borrow, it essentially doubles the amount of money available on an emergency basis to the IMF from some of its members.

The arrangement was spawned by the sudden Mexican crisis two years ago that seemed to threaten the monetary system as it spread to other emerging markets and required a huge global resecue package from the IMF, the United States and others.
The arrangement will go into effect following ratification by the countries and economic entities that have signed on.
"I welcome the New Arrangements to Borrow as a milestone in the membership's efforts to strengthen the IMF," IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said in a statement.
Some 25 countries and institutions have said they are willing to make money available should the IMF need it in a time of upheaval.

They are Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, the Bundesbank, Finland, France, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Italy, Japan, South Korea, Kuwait, Luxembourg, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Norway, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Spain, Sveriges Riksbank, the Swiss National Bank, Thailand, Britain and the United States.
The United States would be the largest contributor, pledging $9.4 billion, although a portion of this must still be approved by Congress.
The so-called G-10 industrial countries, of which there are 11 members, had previously set aside a pool of funds under the so-called General Arrangements to Borrow.
This will be added to by the new members, countries that have made their economic mark more recently in the world and so are being asked to help protect the system.
The Mexican crisis made it clear that the tightly woven economic system can easily spread problems from one country to another and that additional economic muscle was needed to fight these outbreaks.
